questions.q: For a deformation x = χ(X), what does J = det F measure?
questions.a: Ratio of deformed to reference volume, dv/dV
w: Ratio of deformed to reference area, da/dA
Ratio of deformed to reference density, ρ/ρ₀
Square of the largest principal stretch, λ₁²
questions.x: J = det F = dv/dV is the local volume ratio, which must be positive, and mass conservation gives ρJ = ρ₀.

questions.q: A pure rigid rotation F = R is applied. What is C = FᵀF?
questions.x: Since RᵀR = I for a rotation, C = I and the Green-Lagrange strain E = ½(C − I) is zero.

questions.q: Why is ε = ½(∇u + ∇uᵀ) inadequate for a large rigid rotation?
questions.a: It drops ½∇uᵀ∇u, so a pure rotation shows strain
w: It is skew-symmetric, so it contains the rotation itself
It vanishes for every rotation and hides the real strain
It depends on the observer only through the scalar J
questions.x: For u = (R − I)X the in-plane components of ε equal cos θ − 1, while the full E = ½(∇u + ∇uᵀ + ∇uᵀ∇u) is exactly zero for any rotation.

questions.q: Simple shear x₁ = X₁ + γX₂, x₂ = X₂, x₃ = X₃. What is the in-plane block of C?
questions.x: F = [[1,γ],[0,1]], so C = FᵀF = [[1,γ],[γ,1+γ²]], and J = 1 makes simple shear isochoric.

questions.q: A material fiber has unit reference direction N. Its stretch λ is:
questions.x: The deformed fiber is FN, so λ² = |FN|² = N·FᵀFN = N·CN.

questions.q: In the polar decomposition F = RU, what are R and U?
questions.a: R a proper rotation, U a symmetric positive stretch
w: R a symmetric stretch, U a proper orthogonal rotation
R a skew spin tensor, U a symmetric strain rate tensor
R a positive definite stretch, U the volume ratio J times I
questions.x: F = RU with U = √C symmetric positive definite and R = FU⁻¹ proper orthogonal, so the stretch is applied first and then rotated.

questions.q: A bar is stretched so x₁ = 2X₁ with the other directions fixed. Green-Lagrange E_11?
questions.x: E_11 = ½(λ² − 1) = ½(4 − 1) = 1.5, while the engineering strain is λ − 1 = 1.

questions.q: Match each kinematic statement to its meaning
pairs: Deformation gradient mapping dX to dx
questions.x: F maps reference line elements to deformed ones, J = 1 preserves volume, C = I holds exactly for rigid motions, and E = ½(C − I) is the Lagrangian finite strain.

questions.q: Cauchy's theorem: the traction on a plane with unit normal n is:
questions.x: The traction vector is linear in the normal, t = σn, and its normal component is n·σn.

questions.q: Which balance law makes the Cauchy stress symmetric (with zero body couples)?
questions.x: Balance of angular momentum, with zero body couples, gives σ = σᵀ, leaving six independent components.

questions.q: Static local equilibrium in the deformed body with body force b per unit volume:
questions.x: Balance of linear momentum at rest gives div σ + b = 0 pointwise, and σn = t on the traction boundary.

questions.q: Principal stresses are 100, 40 and −20 MPa. Absolute maximum shear stress?
questions.x: Absolute maximum shear is (σ_max − σ_min)/2 = (100 + 20)/2 = 60 MPa, acting on planes at 45° to the 1 and 3 directions.

questions.q: Plane stress: σ_x = 80, σ_y = 20, τ_xy = 40 MPa. Principal stresses?
questions.x: Mohr center (80 + 20)/2 = 50 and radius √(30² + 40²) = 50 give σ₁ = 100 and σ₂ = 0 MPa, with maximum in-plane shear 50 MPa.

questions.q: First Piola-Kirchhoff stress in terms of Cauchy stress σ and F:
questions.x: P = JσF⁻ᵀ gives force per reference area (Nanson's formula), and S = F⁻¹P = JF⁻¹σF⁻ᵀ is the symmetric second Piola stress.

questions.q: Under a change of observer x* = Qx + c (Q a rotation), the Cauchy stress becomes:
questions.x: Cauchy stress is objective, σ* = QσQᵀ, so a frame-indifferent law must satisfy σ̂(QF) = Qσ̂(F)Qᵀ for every rotation Q.

questions.q: Match each stress measure to its description
pairs: Force per reference area, two-point tensor
S = F⁻¹P, symmetric, conjugate to E
questions.x: σ is the true stress, P = JσF⁻ᵀ refers force to reference area, S = F⁻¹P is fully referential and work conjugate to E, and τ = Jσ.

questions.q: Isotropic linear elastic Hooke's law in Lamé form:
questions.x: Isotropy leaves two constants, σ = λ tr(ε)I + 2με, with μ = G the shear modulus.

questions.q: E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.25. What is the shear modulus G?
As ν → 1/2 for an isotropic linear elastic solid:
questions.a: K → ∞, so the solid is incompressible
w: G → ∞, so all shear strains become zero
E → 0 and the solid loses all stiffness
λ → 0 and the Poisson coupling disappears
questions.x: K = E/(3(1 − 2ν)) becomes unbounded as ν → 1/2, so tr ε → 0 and the pressure becomes a reaction found from boundary conditions.

questions.q: Order the count of independent elastic constants from most general to most symmetric
steps: 36: minor symmetries from symmetric σ and ε
21: major symmetry from a strain energy
questions.x: Minor symmetries give 36, a strain energy adds major symmetry for 21, orthotropy gives 9, transverse isotropy 5, and isotropy 2.

questions.q: How many independent elastic constants does a transversely isotropic material have?
questions.x: Transverse isotropy (one axis of rotational symmetry, as in a unidirectional fiber composite) has 5 independent constants.

questions.q: Pure shear stress τ (principal stresses τ, −τ, 0). von Mises equivalent stress?
questions.x: σ_vm = √(½[(2τ)² + τ² + τ²]) = √3 τ, so von Mises predicts shear yield at τ = σ_y/√3.

questions.q: For a two-phase composite, the Voigt and Reuss modulus estimates assume:
questions.a: Voigt equal strain (upper), Reuss equal stress (lower)
w: Voigt equal stress (upper), Reuss equal strain (lower)
Voigt equal strain (lower), Reuss equal stress (upper)
Both equal strain, with different Poisson coupling
questions.x: Voigt (uniform strain, E = Σ f_i E_i) is the upper bound and Reuss (uniform stress, 1/E = Σ f_i/E_i) is the lower bound.

questions.q: Incompressible neo-Hookean solid, σ = −pI + μB. How is the pressure p found?
w: From the constitutive law as p = K tr ε (bulk)
From J = 1 alone, which gives p = μ
From the strain energy alone as p = ∂W/∂J
questions.x: The constraint J = 1 makes p a Lagrange multiplier, fixed by equilibrium and the boundary tractions (for example σ_22 = 0 on free faces in uniaxial tension).

questions.q: Plane strain, isotropic linear elastic body. σ_33 equals:
questions.x: Setting ε_33 = [σ_33 − ν(σ_11 + σ_22)]/E = 0 gives σ_33 = ν(σ_11 + σ_22), the out-of-plane stress that holds a long body at zero axial strain.

questions.q: With zero body force, the Airy stress function φ(x, y) gives:
w: σ_11 = φ,yy, σ_22 = φ,xx, σ_12 = φ,xy
σ_11 = φ,xx, σ_22 = φ,yy, σ_12 = φ,xy
questions.x: These definitions satisfy both in-plane equilibrium equations identically for any smooth φ.

questions.q: Which equation must φ satisfy, and which condition produces it?
questions.x: Equilibrium is built into the Airy definitions, and substituting into the compatibility equation with isotropic Hooke's law gives the biharmonic equation ∇⁴φ = 0.

questions.q: Plate under uniform tension σ₀ along x. Which Airy function gives it?
questions.x: φ = σ₀y²/2 gives σ_11 = φ,yy = σ₀ with σ_22 = σ_12 = 0, since uniform loads need quadratic terms.

questions.q: Which Airy terms solve the end-loaded cantilever (tip shear P, x along the beam)?
questions.x: φ = c₁xy + c₂xy³ gives σ_11 ∝ xy (bending growing linearly with x) and σ_12 = −c₁ − 3c₂y², a parabolic shear that vanishes at y = ±h/2.

questions.q: Why may an Airy solution that matches only end force and moment resultants be used?
questions.a: Saint-Venant: self-equilibrated end loads decay fast
w: Uniqueness guarantees pointwise end tractions are matched
Compatibility redistributes end tractions to match exactly
Maxwell reciprocity makes all end conditions interchangeable
questions.x: By Saint-Venant's principle, statically equivalent end loads give the same stresses beyond a distance of about one section depth from the end.

questions.q: Small circular hole in a large plate under uniaxial tension σ₀. Peak hoop stress?
questions.x: The Kirsch solution gives σ_θθ = 3σ₀ at the hole edge on the diameter perpendicular to the load and −σ₀ at the points on the load axis.

questions.q: Match each plane elasticity item
questions.x: Plane stress suits thin plates, plane strain suits long prismatic bodies, polar Airy gives σ_rr = (1/r)φ,r + (1/r²)φ,θθ, and equibiaxial tension gives K_t = 2 at a circular hole.

questions.q: Thin-walled cylinder, pressure p, radius R, wall t. Hoop stress?
questions.x: A half-cylinder free body gives 2σ_θ tL = 2pRL, so σ_θ = pR/t, twice the axial stress pR/(2t).

questions.q: Thin-walled sphere, pressure p, radius R, wall t. Membrane stress?
questions.x: A hemisphere free body gives σ 2πRt = pπR², so σ = pR/(2t) in every tangential direction.

questions.q: Cylinder with p = 2 MPa, R = 500 mm, t = 10 mm. Hoop and axial stress?
questions.x: σ_θ = pR/t = 2·500/10 = 100 MPa and σ_x = pR/(2t) = 50 MPa, and R/t = 50 is well inside the thin-wall range.

questions.q: Why do longitudinal seams of a pressurized cylinder fail first?
questions.a: They carry hoop stress, twice the axial stress
w: They carry axial stress, twice the hoop stress
They carry end cap bending, twice the hoop
They carry radial stress, which peaks at 2p
questions.x: A longitudinal seam is loaded by the hoop stress pR/t, which is twice the axial stress pR/(2t) carried by circumferential seams.

questions.q: Lamé thick cylinder: general stress solution with constants A and B?
questions.a: σ_rr = A − B/r², σ_θθ = A + B/r²
w: σ_rr = A + B/r², σ_θθ = A + B/r²
σ_rr = A − B ln r, σ_θθ = A + B ln r
σ_rr = A − B/r, σ_θθ = A + B/r
questions.x: Equilibrium plus compatibility give σ_rr = A − B/r² and σ_θθ = A + B/r², with A and B fixed by the inner and outer pressures, and σ_rr + σ_θθ = 2A constant.

questions.q: Thick cylinder under internal pressure only. Where is the hoop stress largest?
questions.x: σ_θθ = A + B/r² with B > 0 is largest at r = a, where σ_θθ = p(a² + b²)/(b² − a²), which exceeds p.

questions.q: Radial equilibrium of an axisymmetric cylinder with zero body force:
questions.x: The cylinder obeys dσ_rr/dr + (σ_rr − σ_θθ)/r = 0, and a sphere carries a factor 2 on the second term because two hoop directions act.

questions.q: Why does a rotating disc need a particular solution beyond the Lamé A, B terms?
questions.a: Body force ρω²r enters radial equilibrium
w: Centrifugal stiffening makes E vary with radius
Coriolis forces add a shear stress σ_rθ
Spin heating adds thermal strain at the rim
questions.x: Radial equilibrium becomes dσ_rr/dr + (σ_rr − σ_θθ)/r + ρω²r = 0, and the body force term gives a particular solution proportional to r².

questions.q: The Euler-Bernoulli kinematic assumption is that cross sections:
questions.a: Remain plane and normal to the deformed axis
w: Remain plane but rotate independently of the axis
Warp so that the shear strain is uniform
Stay normal to the original undeformed axis
questions.x: Plane sections stay plane and normal to the deformed axis, so the axial strain varies linearly through the depth with magnitude yκ and transverse shear strain is zero.

questions.q: Euler-Bernoulli beam: magnitude of bending stress at distance y from the neutral axis?
questions.x: Linear strain yκ times E with M = EIκ gives |σ| = |M|y/I, largest at the extreme fiber.

questions.q: For a beam made of two materials, the neutral axis passes through:
w: The geometric centroid of the cross section
The centroid of the stiffer material alone
The mid-depth of the overall section
questions.x: Zero net axial force, ∫E y κ dA = 0, places the neutral axis at the modulus-weighted centroid, and the bending stiffness is ∫E y² dA.

questions.q: Second moment of area of a b × h rectangle about its base?
questions.x: Parallel axis: I = bh³/12 + bh(h/2)² = bh³/3.

questions.q: Second moment of area of a solid circle of radius r about a diameter?
questions.x: I = πr⁴/4 about any diameter, and the polar moment is J = 2I = πr⁴/2.

questions.q: Unsymmetric section with product of inertia I_yz ≠ 0. A moment about z alone produces:
w: Curvature in the z bending plane alone
Twist of the section about the centroid
Uniform axial strain over the section
questions.x: A nonzero product of inertia couples the bending planes, and along the principal axes (I_yz = 0) each moment produces curvature in its own plane.

questions.q: When does Timoshenko beam theory differ significantly from Euler-Bernoulli?
questions.a: Short, deep beams or low G cores (sandwich)
w: Long, slender beams of high shear modulus metal
Beams loaded in pure bending by end moments
Beams with doubly symmetric cross sections
questions.x: Timoshenko theory adds transverse shear deformation, which matters when depth to length is large or G is low, as in sandwich panels.

questions.q: Propped cantilever (fixed at A, roller at B), uniform load w, span L. Roller reaction?
questions.x: Tip deflection compatibility, wL⁴/(8EI) = RL³/(3EI), gives R = 3wL/8, leaving 5wL/8 at the fixed end.

questions.q: Shear flow magnitude in a thin-walled open section under shear V (principal axes):
questions.a: q = VQ/I, Q = ∫ y t ds from a free edge
w: q = V I/Q, with Q = ∫ y t ds from a free edge
q = V Q/(I t), with Q = ∫ y ds from a free edge
q = V/(A t), uniform around the section
questions.x: Shear flow q = VQ/I builds up from zero at a free edge, thickness enters through Q = ∫ y t ds, and the shear stress is τ = q/t.

questions.q: The shear center of a cross section is the point through which:
questions.a: Transverse load gives bending with zero twist
w: An axial load causes zero bending
The bending stress reaches its maximum value
The web shear flow reaches its peak value, VQ/I
questions.x: Transverse load through the shear center produces pure bending, and a symmetric section has its shear center on the axis of symmetry.

questions.q: Where is the shear center of a thin channel (C) section?
questions.a: Outside the section, beyond the web
w: Inside, at the centroid between the flanges
On the web midline at mid-height
Inside, between the web and the centroid
questions.x: The flange shear flows form a couple that is balanced when the load acts at e = 3b²t_f/(h t_w + 6b t_f) behind the web, on the symmetry axis.

questions.q: Thin semicircular open section of radius R. Shear center distance from the center?
questions.x: Moment balance of the sinusoidal shear flow about the center gives e = 4R/π ≈ 1.27R, beyond the arc on the symmetry axis.

questions.q: Torsion constant of a thin-walled open section made of strips b × t:
questions.x: Each thin strip contributes bt³/3, so open sections have small J and low torsional stiffness GJ.

questions.q: Closed thin square tube, 100 mm midline side, t = 2 mm, T = 1 kN·m. Shear stress?
questions.x: Bredt-Batho: q = T/(2A) = 10⁶/(2·10⁴) = 50 N/mm, so τ = q/t = 25 MPa.

questions.q: A thin circular tube (R/t = 20) is slit along its length. Its torsional stiffness:
w: Falls by a factor of about 20
Falls by a factor of about 3
questions.x: Closed J = 2πR³t and open J = 2πRt³/3, a ratio of 3(R/t)² = 1200, so closed sections are far stiffer in torsion.

questions.q: Match each item of the Prandtl membrane analogy
pairs: Volume under the membrane, T = 2∫ψ dA
questions.x: Shear stress follows the membrane slope, torque follows the enclosed volume, the stress function obeys ∇²ψ = −2Gθ, and a rectangle peaks at the midpoints of its long sides.

questions.q: Castigliano's second theorem for a linear elastic structure:
questions.x: For linear systems the complementary energy equals U, and Δ_i = ∂U/∂P_i gives the displacement at P_i in its direction.

questions.q: Cantilever of length L, tip load P. Bending energy U and tip deflection Δ?
questions.x: U = ∫₀ᴸ (Px)²/(2EI) dx = P²L³/(6EI), and ∂U/∂P = PL³/(3EI).

questions.q: In the method of least work for a statically indeterminate structure:
w: U = 0 at each redundant support, enforcing compatibility
questions.x: Setting ∂U/∂R = 0 states that the displacement at each rigid redundant support is zero, which is the compatibility condition.

questions.q: Put the dummy load procedure for a displacement at an unloaded point in order
steps: Apply a dummy load Q at the point, in the wanted direction
Write M(x) including both the real loads and Q
questions.x: With Q = 0, ∂M/∂Q equals the unit load moment m, so Δ = ∫ mM/(EI) dx, the unit load method.

questions.q: In Rayleigh-Ritz, the trial function must satisfy:
w: Both essential and natural conditions exactly
questions.x: Admissible trial functions satisfy the essential conditions, and the natural conditions emerge approximately from stationarity of Π = U − W.

questions.q: In Rayleigh-Ritz, an elastic spring k supporting a beam at x = a is handled by:
questions.a: Adding ½k w(a)² to the strain energy
w: Forcing w(a) = 0 in the trial function
Adding k w(a) to the external work
Forcing w''(a) = 0 in the trial function
questions.x: A spring support is a natural condition, included as the energy term ½k w(a)² in Π.

questions.q: A one-term Ritz solution for a static displacement problem tends to:
questions.a: Overestimate stiffness, so displacements are too small
w: Underestimate stiffness, so displacements are too large
Give the exact displacement at the load point
questions.x: Restricting the shape adds constraint, so Ritz is too stiff: displacements come out low and buckling loads come out high (upper bounds).

questions.q: Coil spring: G = 80 GPa, wire d = 4 mm, coil radius R = 20 mm, n = 10. Stiffness?
questions.x: The wire twists under T = PR, giving k = Gd⁴/(64R³n) = 80000·256/(64·8000·10) = 4 N/mm.

questions.q: Rigid bar of length L on a base rotational spring C, vertical dead load P at the top. P_cr?
questions.x: Π = ½Cθ² − PL(1 − cos θ) ≈ ½(C − PL)θ² + PLθ⁴/24, and the quadratic coefficient vanishes at P_cr = C/L.

questions.q: For that bar, equilibrium P = Cθ/(L sin θ). The post-buckling behavior is:
questions.a: Stable symmetric bifurcation, P rises with |θ|
w: Unstable symmetric bifurcation, P falls with |θ|
Asymmetric bifurcation, P varies linearly with θ
A limit point with snap-through at P = C/L
questions.x: θ/sin θ ≈ 1 + θ²/6 grows with |θ|, and the positive quartic term PLθ⁴/24 makes the buckled path stable and imperfection insensitive.

questions.q: Match each instability type to its imperfection behavior
questions.x: Stable symmetric systems keep their capacity, unstable symmetric lose it as ε^(2/3) (two-thirds law), asymmetric as ε^(1/2), and limit point systems snap at the load maximum.

questions.q: Effective length factor K for a fixed-free (cantilever) column?
questions.x: P_cr = π²EI/(KL)² with K = 2 for a cantilever, 1 pinned-pinned, 0.7 fixed-pinned and 0.5 fixed-fixed.

questions.q: A pinned-pinned column has P_cr = 100 kN. The same column fixed-fixed?
questions.x: Fixed-fixed has K = 0.5, so P_cr scales by 1/0.5² = 4, giving 400 kN.

questions.q: What characterizes a limit point (shallow arch snap-through)?
questions.a: Load peaks (dP/dθ = 0), then the path jumps
w: Two equilibrium branches intersect at P_cr
The structure stays straight until P_cr
The tangent stiffness keeps rising past P_max
questions.x: At a limit point the single equilibrium path reaches a load maximum with dP/dθ = 0, and the structure snaps dynamically to a distant configuration.

questions.q: A column under a follower (tangential) load should be analyzed with:
questions.a: The kinetic (dynamic) method, load is nonconservative
w: The static energy method using the total potential Π
The adjacent equilibrium method on the straight shape
questions.x: Follower loads are nonconservative, so stability is assessed from the motion equations (kinetic method), which can reveal flutter.

questions.q: A 2-DOF model gives det([[2k − PL, −k],[−k, 2k − PL]]) = 0. Lowest P_cr and mode?
questions.x: 2k − PL = ±k gives PL = k or 3k, the lowest root P_cr = k/L governs, and its eigenvector is θ₁ = θ₂.

boards.prompt: Define F, C and E for a deformation x = χ(X). Then show me why the small strain tensor is inadequate for a large rigid rotation.
points: F = ∂x/∂X maps reference line elements to deformed ones, and J = det F > 0 is the volume ratio
C = FᵀF and E = ½(C − I) measure stretching independent of rigid rotation
A rigid rotation F = R gives C = I and E = 0
ε = ½(∇u + ∇uᵀ) keeps only the linear part of E, so it is valid for small strains and small rotations
For a rotation by θ, ε has in-plane components cos θ − 1, which grow as θ²/2

boards.prompt: Sketch simple shear of a unit square. Write F, find J, and give the stretch of the diagonal fiber.
points: F = [[1,γ],[0,1]] in the shear plane
J = det F = 1, so simple shear is isochoric
λ = √(N·CN) with C = [[1,γ],[γ,1+γ²]]
For N = (1,1)/√2 the stretch is λ = √(1 + γ + γ²/2)
Polar decomposition F = RU separates the rotation R from the stretch U = √C

boards.prompt: Here is a 3D stress state. How do you find the principal stresses and the absolute maximum shear stress?
points: Principal stresses are the eigenvalues of σ, roots of det(σ − sI) = 0
The characteristic equation uses the invariants I₁ = tr σ, I₂, and I₃ = det σ
Principal directions are eigenvectors, mutually orthogonal because σ is symmetric
Absolute maximum shear is (σ_max − σ_min)/2 on planes at 45° to those principal directions
In plane stress, include σ₃ = 0 when choosing σ_max and σ_min

boards.prompt: Distinguish the Cauchy, first Piola and second Piola stresses, and tell me what objectivity requires of a constitutive law.
points: σ is force per deformed area and is symmetric by angular momentum balance
P = JσF⁻ᵀ is force per reference area and is a generally unsymmetric two-point tensor
S = F⁻¹P = JF⁻¹σF⁻ᵀ is symmetric and work conjugate to E
Under a change of observer σ* = QσQᵀ
Frame indifference is satisfied when the response depends on F through C, for example S = Ŝ(C)

boards.prompt: Explain how material symmetry reduces the number of independent elastic constants from 81 down to 2.
points: C_ijkl in σ_ij = C_ijkl ε_kl has 81 components
Symmetry of σ and ε (minor symmetries) reduces this to 36
A strain energy W gives major symmetry C_ijkl = C_klij, leaving 21
Orthotropy leaves 9 and transverse isotropy leaves 5
Isotropy leaves 2, for example λ and μ or E and ν

boards.prompt: Split a stress state into hydrostatic and deviatoric parts and connect each part to the elastic moduli and to yield.
points: σ = σ_m I + s with σ_m = tr σ/3 and s the deviator
σ_m = K tr ε and s = 2G e, with K = E/(3(1 − 2ν)) = λ + 2μ/3 and G = E/(2(1 + ν))
von Mises σ_vm = √(3J₂) with J₂ = ½ s:s depends only on the deviator
Metal yield is governed by the deviatoric part, so superposed hydrostatic pressure leaves the yield prediction unchanged
Tresca uses the maximum shear (σ_max − σ_min)/2 = σ_y/2

boards.prompt: Set up an Airy stress function solution for a cantilever with a tip shear load. Which polynomial terms do you pick, and how do you apply the boundary conditions?
points: Take φ = c₁xy + c₂xy³, which satisfies ∇⁴φ = 0
Top and bottom faces are traction free: σ_22 = σ_12 = 0 at y = ±h/2, applied as t = σn on each face
At the loaded end impose the resultant ∫σ_12 t dy = P and zero axial force and moment
Saint-Venant's principle justifies resultant-only end conditions away from the ends
The result is a bending stress linear in x and y and a parabolic shear stress, matching beam theory

boards.prompt: A large plate with a small circular hole is pulled in uniaxial tension. Describe how you solve it and what the stress concentration is.
points: Use polar coordinates with σ_rr = (1/r)φ,r + (1/r²)φ,θθ and σ_θθ = φ,rr
Far-field uniaxial stress σ₀ splits into an axisymmetric part and a cos 2θ part
The hole surface is traction free: σ_rr = σ_rθ = 0 at r = a
Kirsch gives σ_θθ = 3σ₀ at the hole edge perpendicular to the load and −σ₀ on the load axis
The concentration is local and decays to the far field within a few hole radii, and equibiaxial tension gives K_t = 2

boards.prompt: Derive the hoop and axial stresses in a thin-walled pressurized cylinder and tell me when the result is valid.
points: Half-cylinder free body: 2σ_θ tL = p(2R)L, so σ_θ = pR/t
End cap free body: σ_x 2πRt = pπR², so σ_x = pR/(2t)
Thin-wall theory holds for t/R of about 1/10 or less, where radial stress (order p) is small compared with pR/t
Hoop stress is twice axial, so longitudinal seams are the critical ones
A sphere of the same R and t carries pR/(2t), half the cylinder hoop stress

boards.prompt: For a thick-walled cylinder under internal pressure, set up and solve for the stresses. Then tell me how a spinning disc changes the problem.
points: Equilibrium dσ_rr/dr + (σ_rr − σ_θθ)/r = 0 combined with compatibility and Hooke's law
Solution σ_rr = A − B/r² and σ_θθ = A + B/r²
Boundary conditions σ_rr(a) = −p and σ_rr(b) = 0 fix A and B
Maximum hoop stress is at the inner wall, σ_θθ(a) = p(a² + b²)/(b² − a²)
A rotating disc adds the body force ρω²r, requiring a particular solution proportional to r²

boards.prompt: Derive the bending relation for a beam made of two bonded materials and tell me where the neutral axis is.
points: Plane sections remain plane and normal, so the axial strain is linear in y with magnitude yκ
Stress in each material is σ = E_i ε, so stress jumps at the interface
Zero net axial force, ∫E y dA = 0, places the neutral axis at the modulus-weighted centroid
M = (∫E y² dA)κ, so the effective bending stiffness is the modulus-weighted EI
The parallel axis theorem I = I_c + A d² assembles each part about the neutral axis

boards.prompt: I apply a vertical load to an unequal-leg angle section beam. What happens, and how do you compute the stresses? When would you switch to Timoshenko theory?
points: The product of inertia I_yz couples bending, so the beam deflects out of the load plane
Either rotate to principal axes (I_yz = 0) and superpose, or use the coupled formula with I_y, I_z and I_yz
The neutral axis is inclined relative to the moment axis
Bending with zero twist requires the load to act through the shear center
Timoshenko theory adds shear deformation, important for short, deep beams or low G cores

boards.prompt: Find the shear center of a channel section and explain why it sits where it does.
points: Assume the shear V acts through the shear center and compute q = VQ/I with Q = ∫ y t ds from each free edge
Flange shear flow varies linearly and web shear flow parabolically
The flange shear flow resultants form a couple about the web
Moment balance about the web gives e = 3b²t_f/(h t_w + 6b t_f)
The shear center lies on the symmetry axis, outside the section beyond the web

boards.prompt: Compare the torsion of a thin closed tube with the same tube slit open. Then use the membrane analogy to tell me where the peak stress is in a rectangular bar.
points: Closed section: Bredt-Batho q = T/(2A_enclosed) and J = 4A²/∮(ds/t)
Open section: J = Σ bt³/3, with stress varying linearly through the thickness
For a circular tube the stiffness ratio is 3(R/t)², so closed sections are far stiffer
Prandtl ∇²ψ = −2Gθ with T = 2∫ψ dA; shear stress follows the membrane slope and torque follows its volume
In a rectangle the peak shear stress is at the midpoints of the long sides and the corners carry zero stress; τ = Tr/J applies to circular sections

boards.prompt: Find the deflection at a point of a frame where no external load acts, using an energy method. What changes if the frame is statically indeterminate?
points: Apply a dummy load Q at the point in the direction of the wanted displacement
Δ = ∂U/∂Q evaluated at Q = 0, which equals ∫ M(∂M/∂Q)/(EI) dx
Equivalently, unit load method: δ = ∫ mM/(EI) dx with m from a unit load
For linear systems Castigliano uses complementary energy, which equals U
For indeterminate frames, least work ∂U/∂R = 0 for each redundant enforces compatibility

boards.prompt: Use Rayleigh-Ritz to estimate the deflection of a beam with a spring support at one end. What does the approximation guarantee?
points: Π = U − W with U = ½∫EI(w'')² dx + ½k w(end)²
The trial function satisfies the essential (kinematic) boundary conditions
Spring supports, moments and shears are natural conditions included through energy
dΠ/da_i = 0 gives the coefficients
One-term Ritz is too stiff: displacements low, buckling loads high; springs combine as 1/k = Σ1/kᵢ in series and k = Σkᵢ in parallel

boards.prompt: A rigid bar with a base rotational spring carries a vertical load. Find the critical load and characterize the post-buckling behavior and imperfection sensitivity.
points: Π = ½Cθ² − PL(1 − cos θ), with cos θ ≈ 1 − θ²/2 + θ⁴/24
Equilibrium dΠ/dθ = 0 and stability d²Π/dθ² > 0
The quadratic term ½(C − PL)θ² vanishes at P_cr = C/L
The quartic term PLθ⁴/24 is positive, so the bifurcation is stable symmetric
Stable symmetric systems are imperfection insensitive, while unstable symmetric ones lose capacity ∝ ε^(2/3)

boards.prompt: Two rigid bars joined by rotational springs carry an axial load. How do you get the critical load and the mode shapes, and how does buckling differ from yielding?
points: A hinge spring between bars stores ½C(θ₂ − θ₁)², a base spring stores ½Cθ₁²
Expand Π to quadratic order in the angles and form the stiffness (Hessian) matrix
Set its determinant to zero; the lowest root is the critical load
Eigenvectors give the mode shapes
Buckling is a stiffness phenomenon set by E and geometry, while yielding is set by material strength σ_y
